This is a course that is mandatory for most students, regardless of their major. As such, one would expect the instructor to be understanding of the fact that most students have no desire to be in that classroom. Self-awareness, I believe, is an important skill, particularly in the context of a professional communication course. The structure of the course itself is inherently flawed in how outdated it is, and while this is an issue entirely out of the instructor's control, it remains that Ms Erbil refused to allow herself to be aware of this fact. For someone who constantly pushed the idea of not taking things personally, she, without fail, took students' actions as a personal attack. She emphasised punctuality in a manner that can be described as overzealous at best; being even a minute late could bar you from her classroom. She demanded students' full attention, while teaching the class in a manner that caused boredom to the point of despair. She constantly made references to Turkish pop culture and played videos in Turkish without any subtitles, despite being aware of the international students in her classroom and taking offense if those students let their attention wander. Ms Erbil had a rather alarming tendency to be unprofessional. A few highlights: she casually mentioned having hit a "small child" while driving; it remains a mystery whether the child is okay or not. The way she handled the sexual harassment portion of the course was simply atrocious; she said that men should be careful of what they say because anything can be misconstrued as harassment—I do wonder what the implications of that statement were. When a student said he wore shorts to an interview, she commented on the unprofessional choice he made and followed it up with an unimaginably unprofessional question: "what did the interviewer say about your nice long legs?". This was before the sexual harassment section, of course, so perhaps she simply misspoke.

Over the course of this semester, I found myself, time and time again, astonished at the existence and implementation of a course that was so unfailingly and utterly useless. This course had no business being mandatory; in fact, I would argue that this course had no business existing at all. There was not a single aspect of this course that could possibly be of use to anyone—particularly because most of the students were well past their first-year. The course was structured only with consideration to those who wanted to go into corporate jobs; it was an entirely unwelcome thrust into a world of corporate policies that most of us wanted no part of. It seemed akin to fourteen-week long HR seminar—unnecessary and unproductive, with a healthy dose of the ability to make everything exponentially worse. The better parts of this course were simply useless; others, however, were actively harmful. The idea of high-context versus low-context cultures is merely a poor attempt at masking what I believe most of us would call "racism."

This course does teach some important fundamental skills like professional communication, CV and personal statement preparations, etc., but I believe it would be more widely accessible and useful if it were either differentiated based on what field students wanted to go into, or it could be formatted as a seminar/workshop course without the added and unnecessary burdens of group work and a lot of corporate strategies that are only important to a handful of students.

This class has some crucial aspects that get us ready for the real world, and I know I'll be looking back at these slides for the rest of my life. That being said, group projects can really hurt the efforts of people who actually put the work in. I guess dealing with that is just one of the lessons of both this class and life in general. I just wish I had a better group so we could have created something more meaningful and productive.

I will start professionally, as she would've wanted. Putting aside the ridiculous triviality of the course itself, the instructor was extremely uptight and maintained her artifically crafted "professional" façade for four months straight. She constantly told us to be professional and do things the way the "real world" works. There is a big flaw in this, however, as I am sure she is not aware of the real world whatsoever. My department, which I will not disclose, does not require me to be as uptight as she would expect. I have never encountered any professor or work manager who has expected me to be the plastic capitalistic doll that she thinks is the solution to professionalism. 
Aside from that, she has a very ableist view of people, and clearly does not understand neurodivergent struggles, as she stated multiple times that we could just "work on it". 
She has no understanding of the "real" world because she is bound up in her own tightly created artifical world that believes a suit and a wide plastered smile will fix every world problem to ever exist. 
I know her intentions are not evil, I just think she needs to reconsider the way she teaches this class and engages with her students.

Deniz Erbil hoca has a very passive approach towards the "modern professional world." Instead of focusing on helping us present ourselves in ways that fit our personalities as well as our fields of interest & study, she is constantly trying to change us for "our own good" because the professional world is "harsh." She appears to not be aware that people like her keeping those standards are the reason the professional world is not as accepting as it needs to be in this day and age. Again, she is not aware that students in creative people WILL look, present, and act creative, saying things that imply that they have less chance of appearing professional out there. HOWEVER, STUDENTS IN CREATIVE FIELDS WILL BE HIRED BY SIMILARLY "CREATIVE" PEOPLE. She is trying to convince us that everyone needs to fit in one single mold to appear professional. Another thing is that she does not fully understand or acknowledge neurodivergent people's struggles that are clearly out of their will and not even a problem in the real world at this point. EVEN if it were a problem, professional leaders such as herself are the ones responsible for making the professional field a safe and normal space for everyone instead of constantly trying to tell neurodivergent people to just "work on it" because "it's not professional." Still, I understand her approach that she is trying to prepare students for the "real world," but she does not need to conform to such standards, especially when the students are trying to make a point and make a difference.
